entries.title: Xi’s greatest power is what he chooses not to do
entries.summary: As Trump and Putin struggle to end their wars, China is gaining influence through restraint.
entries.content:
As Trump and Putin struggle to end their wars, China is gaining influence through restraint.

Before Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for their first trilateral summit in Shenzhen, commentators were already asking whether this would be “Yalta 2.0”: three great powers dividing the world and deciding the fate of smaller nations. When a reporter put the question to Putin, the Russian president paused and nodded. Xi, meanwhile, urged the three countries to abandon “Cold War thinking”. Recalling how they had “fought side by side” during World War II, he declared: “when major countries live in harmony, the world enjoys peace; when major countries clash, the world falls into turmoil.”

The summit produced the China-Russia-US Declaration toward Peace, rather than the carve-up some had predicted. But the meeting also revealed a striking difference between the three leaders. Two were mired in wars they could not bring to a satisfactory end, while the third was fighting neither. Beijing had the weight to change the others’ odds and had chosen not to use it.

Trump came to Shenzhen fresh from a midterm rout that handed both chambers of Congress to the Democrats. He is also waging a war against Iran he cannot win outright. Since it erupted in February, the conflict has rattled oil and energy supplies, drawn in the Houthis in Yemen and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. He arrived, by one account, no longer chasing votes but achievements, a president running out of options. Putin came trailing a war in Ukraine now in its fifth year, isolated by the West and with an economy losing momentum.

Ukraine was on the agenda: the three discussed the war at the American president’s initiative. Yet the American envoys tasked with ending it, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, travelled to Berlin to brief Ukraine and European leaders, who were determined not to be excluded from decisions about the war. Zelenskyy, awaiting his debrief there, put it plainly: issues concerning Ukraine must be decided with Ukraine, and those concerning Europe, with Europe. Any agreement reached in Shenzhen would still have to contend with the demands of those directly involved in the conflict.

Beijing’s position on Ukraine offers another perspective on the war. Chinese officials have posed the counterfactual plainly: had China chosen to arm Russia, the front would not look as it does today. Strategists describe its approach as “constructive neutrality”, arguing that siding openly would have widened the war, while China’s own red lines lowered the nuclear temperature.

Meanwhile, the fighting continued. As the leaders met, Russian drones hit Kharkiv, and Ukraine struck oil facilities in Tatarstan and hit the Kerch Bridge for the third time in a week. The war was being settled not at the diplomatic table but on the ground, which is exactly why a room in Shenzhen could not carve it up.

China’s reluctance to accept commitments on other powers’ terms was also apparent in the nuclear discussions. Washington has long sought a trilateral nuclear arms control framework involving Russia and China, but Beijing has refused to join on equal terms. Its arsenal, at an estimated 620 warheads, is a fraction of the American and Russian stockpiles of some 5,000 each, a disparity Beijing cites in declining equal terms.

The declaration the three leaders issued covered UN reform, more refined oil supply, opposition to what they described as abuses of jurisdiction by the International Criminal Court, and a pledge that a nuclear war “cannot be won and must never be fought”. Critics called it the lowest common denominator. They were right about the limited substance, but Beijing had managed to convene the other two powers on its own terms, without agreeing to the division of the world that some had anticipated.

China today occupies the position the United States held before 1914 and again before 1939: the power whose restraint, more than anyone’s force, is setting the terms. The heft is real: on purchasing-power terms the largest economy on Earth, a manufacturing base roughly equal to the G7 combined, a military leading in a growing list of categories. China could alter the trajectory of the wars now being fought. Each, in its own way, runs through Beijing: the war in Ukraine, the confrontation with Iran and the turbulence spilling across the Middle East.

Beijing’s treatment of Trump at the summit was revealing. Diminished at home and abroad, he was given centre stage: a welcome on the tarmac, a front-row seat at the group photograph and a state banquet. Commentators called it a host humbling a supplicant, but it was the weakened guest who was being given a platform. Offering Trump dignity was not a sign of submission. Beijing could afford to do so while conserving its leverage.

China, however, is not without vulnerabilities. It faces a tightening security arc along its periphery, a property market still working through weakness, a youth jobs problem and a military still reckoning with corruption in its own ranks. Beijing’s “constructive” posture is in part a judgement that exercising its influence too freely would expose its limits.

The smaller economies of the region, the ones the Yalta frame assumes are being carved up, are, if anything, the beneficiaries. Their stability is a by-product of a restraint they had no hand in negotiating. That is a strange thing to call domination.

Yalta was powers carving up a world they then fought over. Shenzhen was different: leaders unable to finish their wars gathered before one who could tip the balance but had chosen not to. Xi expressed confidence that the seeds planted at the meeting would eventually bear fruit, a bet, not a result.

The “Yalta 2.0” label endures because it is a flattering story, but the world on display in Shenzhen is not governed; it is balanced. China’s greatest power may lie in the wars it has chosen not to enter and its refusal to end them on terms set by others.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

entries.title: UK says new deal will ‘rebuild bridges’ with EU: What’s in it?
entries.summary: Agreements aim to simplify trade checks, link emissions systems and launch a youth mobility programme.
entries.content:
Agreements aim to simplify trade checks, link emissions systems and launch a youth mobility programme.

The United Kingdom and the European Union have struck a deal aimed at mending fences and repairing the economic fallout caused by Brexit, a decade after UK voters opted to leave the bloc.

At a joint news conference following the EU-UK summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the deal would “rebuild the bridges that were broken all those years ago”. He hailed the agreements as “a good deal for Britain”.

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said there was an “intensive” debate on how much the world has changed since Brexit, during the meeting.

The COVID pandemic “was not even over when Russia started the war in Ukraine”, she said. “We have stuck together from day one on.

“We can always work on an incremental improvement of our relationship, but as I said, we are totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture.”

The agreements cover three areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies.

But disagreements remain, particularly over university tuition fees.

Burnham also faces political resistance at home over how far strengthening ties with the EU should go.

Here is what you need to know:

What do we know so far?

Three main agreements were on the table at the summit between Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

The first would remove checks and reduce paperwork on food and agricultural products traded between Britain and the EU, making exports easier and potentially lowering costs for businesses and consumers. That could be good news for businesspeople like Tim Jones, an English cheesemaker whom Al Jazeera recently interviewed.

The second would link the two sides’ emissions-trading systems, which would give an exemption to goods from Britain and the EU, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.

The third establishes a youth mobility programme allowing up to 100,000 people under 30 from each side to live in the other’s territory for up to three years for work, study or travel.

Burnham said the agreements could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s gross domestic product (GDP), raising his previous estimate of 0.4 percent.

The prime minister described the package as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people”.

What are the sticking points?

Despite the breakthrough, hurdles remain, among them university tuition fees. Brussels wants EU students attending British universities to pay the same domestic rates as British students rather than the substantially higher international fees currently charged.

London has resisted the proposal, which could have significant financial implications for universities.

“We have not yet reached an agreement on tuition fees, and we have given ourselves six months to reach that agreement,” an EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters.

Another unresolved issue concerns Britain’s demand for access to the EU’s “made in Europe” rules, notably for cars.

“Made in Europe” is part of the EU’s planned Industrial Accelerator Act and is aimed primarily at forcing Chinese automakers to produce cars within the bloc using local suppliers in order to qualify for key subsidies and bid for government procurement contracts.

The EU has indicated it is willing to grant this but on the condition that London aligns with its policies, which restrict imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

What can we expect next?

More wrangling, talks and negotiations.

Burnham has indicated that his government will examine longer-term options, ranging from maintaining existing arrangements to joining the EU customs union or eventually rejoining the bloc.

“After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship,” he said.

But rejoining would require support from British voters and unanimous approval from EU member states, making any immediate return unlikely.

Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from Brussels, said there was “no actual signing” expected on Friday. “There’s no document being inked,” she said.

A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera, “As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place … and talks will continue on some areas.”

Where do other UK political parties stand?

The negotiations have divided the UK’s political landscape.

Within Burnham’s Labour Party, some politicians support rebuilding European ties but fear reopening the divisive Brexit debate.

“I’m happy with closer ties, but he does need to tread carefully,” one Labour MP told the AFP news agency.

The opposition Conservatives and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK have predictably criticised the government’s direction. “I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again,” Farage, who led the Brexit campaign, told the BBC.

He warned that the discussion would soon become one about whether Britain should rejoin the EU.

A YouGov poll published on Wednesday suggested 54 percent of UK citizens think “it would be acceptable to have a rejoin referendum in the next five years” but are divided over whether it is a top priority.

European officials, meanwhile, have remained cautious about Britain’s longer-term intentions.

Sonja Hyland, Ireland’s ambassador in London, said there was “a lack of clarity” about what Brexit meant. If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants”.

entries.title: Spain court grants bail to pro-Palestinian activist James ‘Fergie’ Chambers
entries.summary: The philanthropist is accused by US authorities of financially supporting Hamas.
entries.content:
The philanthropist is accused by US authorities of financially supporting Hamas.

A court in Spain has granted conditional bail to American James “Fergie” Chambers, a pro-Palestine philanthropist who is accused of financially supporting Hamas, and is the subject of an ongoing extradition request by the United States government.

Chambers left Aranjuez prison near Madrid on Friday afternoon, shortly after Spain’s High Court ordered him released.

“This is wonderful news that our request for bail has been granted. My client has been imprisoned for nearly five months without having been convicted of any crime, and in the absence of credible evidence to support the US charges. We hope the National Court will reject this baseless extradition request,” said Aitor Martinez, Chambers’s lawyer, in a statement.

The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas. He is not charged with any “terrorism” offences and denies any wrongdoing.

Translation problems

In a recent legal development, lawyers for Chambers said mistranslations between the US criminal charge in English and the version presented to Spanish authorities in Spanish made the allegations seem more serious.

After a hearing last week, the court had been expected to rule on the extradition request in the coming weeks, but it said on Friday that the translation errors could delay a final decision.

The High Court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent’s sworn statement, submitted in support of the extradition request.

“The US authorities’ admission that they made ‘substantial’ changes to the extradition documents when translating them into Spanish raises grave concerns that the evidence was manipulated to mislead the Spanish authorities about the seriousness of the allegations against my client,” said Martinez.

“This further demonstrates why the UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders has warned that Fergie would face ‘irreparable human rights violations’ if extradited to the US and has called for the extradition request to be rejected.”

Asylum claim pending

Chambers, the heir to the Cox Enterprises media fortune and worth a reported $250m, was arrested on an Interpol Red Notice in Ibiza in July, but has since applied for asylum in Spain.

He cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited from Spain to the US at all.

Chambers’s wife, Stella Schnabel, previously told Al Jazeera that she was appealing to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to intervene on their behalf and grant an expedited asylum request.

“If [Sanchez] chooses not to act, he risks enabling [US President Donald] Trump to establish a precedent in Spain and across Europe which criminalises solidarity with the Palestinian people,” she said.

entries.title: Trump, Putin, Xi pledge to increase global petrol supplies – but how?
entries.summary: Analysts are sceptical about how this will be achieved amid the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran.
entries.content:
Analysts are sceptical about how this will be achieved amid the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran.

The United States, China and Russia have pledged to increase petrol supplies as the wars in Iran – started by Israel and the US – and Ukraine – started by Russia – continue to upend global energy markets.

Following their trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said in a joint statement that they “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”.

The three leaders also “reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows”.

But analysts are sceptical about how this will actually work amid the US having little to no spare refining capacity, Russia being constrained by continued Ukrainian attacks on its energy infrastructure and China’s crude oil imports disrupted by the US and Israel’s war on Iran.

“The trilateral statement should be treated as political noise rather than the first step to boosting global fuel supplies,” Hamad Hussain, a senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera.

“The announcement sounds like it is designed to placate consumers and constituencies. Previous efforts to increase supply [like the US-Russian diesel deal] went nowhere,” Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera.

So is what the three leaders said impossible?

Here’s what we know:

How big are these countries’ refineries?

China and the US are the world’s biggest oil refiners by capacity, followed by Russia and India.

China

China has roughly 18.5 to 18.83 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil refining capacity. But refining in the country is dependent on its crude oil imports, which have been badly disrupted by the continuing US-Iran conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, through which Gulf oil exporters normally ship crude oil – much of it to Asia.

According to a November report by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crude oil refinery imports in China fell by 2.1 million bpd in the second quarter of 2026 and by an additional 0.8 million barrels bpd in the third quarter of the year.

United States

As of January 1 this year, the US had an operable crude oil distillation capacity of about 18.16 million bpd. Production has increased since the war began, and is already running at near full capacity.

According to an October EIA report, “the US refinery fleet has run at higher-than-normal rates this year, with refinery utilisation averaging more than 95 percent of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998”.

Russia

Russia has roughly 6.5 million bpd of oil refining capacity, according to the International Energy Agency.

But Ukrainian drone strikes on its energy infrastructure have severely impacted its refining capacity. “In June, Russian refinery throughput fell to 3.8 million barrels per day, its lowest level in more than 20 years and roughly 30 percent below a year earlier,” a September International Energy Agency report noted.

India

Meanwhile, India has an oil refining capacity of about 5.36 million bpd, according to government figures. But New Delhi is also heavily dependent on crude oil imports, and this has been affected by blockades in the Strait of Hormuz.

Can the US refine more petroleum?

According to the EIA, US refineries are currently running at close to maximum capacity.

This has been driven largely by “tight global supplies for distillate fuel oil, leading to high international demand for US distillate fuel oil exports”, a November EIA report states. Distillate fuel oil is refined petroleum which includes diesel fuels and light fuel oils.

Hussain said that while it may be profitable to refine more oil amid higher oil prices this year, the issue is that Washington “does not have spare capacity” to do so.

The Trump administration says it is determined to boost global fuel supply and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said his department is “talking about reopening every refinery we can” to do so.

According to a November 19 Reuters report, US refiner Valero Energy agreed to buy the century-old LyondellBasell Industries refinery near Houston, Texas, in October and restore a portion of the facility, adding 165,000 bpd of processing capacity by the end of 2027.

The plan would reverse years of refinery closures in the US and add about 1 percent to overall US refining capacity of 18 million bpd, Reuters reported. But analysts say the total price tag of acquiring and recommissioning this refinery could reach $1bn.

Can Russia increase supplies?

Since last year, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have resulted in serious fuel shortages across the country.

According to the IEA, in the first eight months of 2026, a Russian refinery was hit on average once every three days.

Reuters has reported that drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October and several regions have also begun limiting fuel.

On Friday, Reuters also reported that the Russia-installed governor of Crimea’s Sevastopol region, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said petrol sales there were being limited to one full car tank and 20 litres (5.3 gallons) in jerrycans at a number of pumping stations from Thursday.

He said the measures were being introduced to prevent people from filling canisters with hundreds of litres at a time, causing queues and preventing others from refilling.

The Siberian city of Tomsk also capped sales of petrol and diesel to 30 and 50 litres, respectively, from last week, according to local authorities.

On Thursday, the city of Penza, 770km (480 miles) southeast of Moscow, restricted petrol sales to 50 litres while limiting diesel to 200 litres per vehicle. At least half a dozen other regions introduced restrictions earlier this month.

With Ukrainian attacks continuing and Russia limiting fuel, refining more is currently a challenge for the country.

According to a November EIA report, Russia is also a major fuel exporter, especially of diesel. So any issues with its refining and decline in its exports will have a global impact.

While Trump and Putin agreed on a deal in October to allow some Russian diesel exports, none of the shipped fuel has reached customers, as traders have refused to take it.

The EIA noted that Russia’s loss of refinery operations has also “reduced refining activity in Asia and the Middle East, contributing to diesel prices increasing to the highest nominal levels on record in September”.

Can China make up the gap?

The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz strained crude oil imports to China earlier this year, but these have largely recovered.

While Beijing does not officially disclose the volumes of crude flowing into or out of its strategic and commercial stockpiles, Reuters reported that the world’s largest crude importer saw arrivals of 9.88 million bpd in October, up 9.4 percent from September’s 9.03 million bpd and the most since March, just after the war began.

Before the Iran war began on February 28, China was purchasing an average of 10.5 million barrels of crude per day by sea, according to sea-borne commodity data group Vortexa.

China also began stockpiling crude oil in October as imports recovered.

According to Hussain, “China does have some spare refinery capacity it could utilise”.

“But given that petrol and diesel inventories appear to be low in China, any increase in refined output may be used to replenish reserves rather than for export, which would keep global fuel supply constrained,” he said.

“In any case, the return of refined output from the Middle East will be key to lowering global fuel prices,” he added.

entries.title: Myanmar, China object to landmark ICJ ruling on Rohingya genocide
entries.summary: A Myanmar government spokesperson said the ruling was unjust and noted that the court's decision was not unanimous.
entries.content:
A Myanmar government spokesperson said the ruling was unjust and noted that the court’s decision was not unanimous.

Myanmar’s government has rejected a ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that its security forces conducted state-sponsored genocide against the country’s Rohingya minority, calling the judgement “unfair”.

Myanmar’s government spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe told a news conference on Friday that the military government was a victim of injustice. China also criticised the verdict, a day after issuing a statement alongside the United States and Russia calling on international bodies such as the ICJ to refrain from abusing their jurisdiction.

The statements follow an ICJ ruling on Thursday that said Buddhist-majority Myanmar had committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority in a crackdown in 2017.

“Our country was unjustly accused,” Soe said. “This ⁠⁠decision is not a ⁠⁠unanimous decision by everyone; it is not fair.”

China, which is allied to Myanmar’s military government, said that such rulings by the UN’s top court are “not conducive to the settlement of disputes”.

“The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.

The ICJ found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women, and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called “clearance operations”.

Of the court’s 15 judges, nine ruled in favour of declaring genocide and six ruled against. It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges had determined that a state committed genocide.

One of the court’s judges is Chinese and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.

The brutal crackdown launched by Myanmar security forces nine years ago forced about 700,000 Rohingya to seek refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. Some also fled further afield, including to Malaysia.

The ICJ’s ruling said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined later, and it must also allow the “safe and dignified return” of Rohingya displaced as a ⁠⁠result of Myanmar’s “wrongful acts”.

On Friday, Malaysia said it plans to resettle 10,000 Rohingya migrants in Turkiye as part of efforts to resolve the long-running refugee challenge it has faced.

Rohingya people make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

Myanmar is in the grip of a multi-fronted civil war, including in Rakhine state where most of the country’s Rohingya lived.

entries.title: Iraqi forces deploy to Jurf al-Sakhar after deal with Iran-backed group
entries.summary: Iraq's Federal Police are due to assume control of town's newly established control headquarters.
entries.content:
Iraq’s Federal Police are due to assume control of town’s newly established control headquarters.

Iraqi security forces have been deployed to Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the powerful Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah armed group.

Security forces arrived in the town, which sits in Babil province about 60km southwest of Baghdad and is also known as Jurf al-Nasr, on Friday.

The deployment, which is understood to have been driven by pressure from the United States and its Gulf allies, comes a day after a compromise deal was sealed that will see Kataib Hezbollah move to other areas of the country.

The government announced on Monday that it would take control of Jurf al-Sakhar after a probe raised suspicions that the group had stolen hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iraqi oil via illicit oil refineries.

It gave the group, which is believed to have thousands of trained fighters, a deadline of Friday to leave the town. However, under Thursday’s deal, they are expected to withdraw from the area within a month.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, has denied the allegations of stealing oil. Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following the investigation into alleged oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar.

Analysts suspect the push for withdrawal is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus. Baghdad has also come under pressure from the US to reduce Iran’s influence in the country.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has had to tread a fine line as he seeks to contain Kataib Hezbollah without triggering a confrontation.

Al-Zaidi said on Friday, as he addressed the government forces entering the town, that they were “not waging war”.

“Everyone present there are your brothers,” he told the troops, “the sons of this nation, and their blood is our blood.”

However, he insisted that his decision to restrict weapons to state control was final.

Tricky talks

Under the compromise, a combined force comprising an Iraqi army brigade, a Federal Police battalion and an Energy Police regiment will provide protection for oil pipelines in the area.

Two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are part of Iraq’s official security forces, will also participate.

Lieutenant General Ahmed Hatem Hamid said on Friday that a control headquarters had been established in Jurf al-Sakhar and that the Federal Police would control the facility, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

Iraq’s Energy Police have also begun securing an oil pipeline running through Jurf al-Sakhar, INA reported.

Baghdad-based security and strategic analyst Fadel Abu Raghif told Al Jazeera that the deal for Iraqi security forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar came after lengthy and delicate talks with Kataib Hezbollah.

The agreement followed “in-depth negotiations, and after wrangling and a tug of war that lasted about two months or so,” Abu Raghif said.

Highlighting the delicacy of the situation, Esmail Qaani, the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force, had visited Iraq earlier this week to help defuse tension and seal the deal.

Kataib Hezbollah helped recapture Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) and has had a large presence in the town for more than a decade.

Reporting from Babil province, Al Jazeera’s Samer Al Kobeisi said the departure of Kataib Hezbollah would allow the reopening of an area that has been closed for about 12 years, according to the government.

entries.title: Nations League quarterfinal draw: Spain face France, England play Norway
entries.summary: World Cup winners and European champions Spain have reached three of the four Nations League finals, winning in 2023.
entries.content:
World Cup winners and European champions Spain have reached three of the four Nations League finals, winning in 2023.

World champions Spain will face France while England will play Norway in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League after the draw took place on Friday.

Spain beat France 2-0 in the semifinals of the World Cup in the United States in July on the way to winning the trophy. They also defeated Les Bleus 5-4 in the semifinals of the last edition of the Nations League last year.

The quarterfinals will be played over two legs in late March with Spain at home first after coming second in Group A3 while France topped Group A1.

Spain won the Nations League in 2023 while France beat them to win the 2021 final.

England topped Group A3 on goal difference after beating Spain away in their last outing, and their reward is a two-legged last-eight tie with Norway with the first leg on Norwegian soil.

England edged Norway in the World Cup quarterfinals this year before losing to Argentina in the semifinals.

The other quarterfinal ties will pit reigning Nations League champions Portugal against the Netherlands and Belgium against Germany.

The winners of the quarterfinals will advance to the final stages, which will be held in June at a venue yet to be decided.

Spain or France will play the Netherlands or Portugal in the single-leg semis, and England would face Belgium or Germany should they get past Norway.
